extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's text)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and criteria about discrete valuations, discrete valuation rings (DVRs), smooth/étale morphisms, valuative criteria for separatedness/properness, and related facts about regular local rings and filtrations. Includes definitions, theorem-statements, exercises, and proof sketches used to identify and verify these properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: discrete valuation on a field
rubrics_metrics.description: A discrete valuation on K is a surjective homomorphism v : K^× → Z (in particular, v(xy)=v(x)+v(y)) satisfying v(x+y) ≥ min(v(x),v(y)) except if x+y=0. It is often convenient to say v(0)=∞. More generally a valuation is a surjective homomorphism v : K^× → G to a totally ordered abelian group G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (i) 5-adic valuation on Q (power of 5 in a rational), (ii) for K=k(x) the power of x in a rational function, (iii) for K=k(x) the negative of the degree (same as (ii) with x↦1/x). (Also remark about Puiseux series giving non-discrete valuations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation ring and its basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a valuation v, the set Ov = {x in K : v(x) ≥ 0} is a ring called the valuation ring of v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The set {x in K : v(x) > 0} is the unique maximal ideal of Ov (show complement elements are invertible), hence Ov is a local ring. Exercises invite describing Ov in the three examples and verifying maximal ideal uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: discrete valuation ring (DVR)
rubrics_metrics.description: An integral domain A is called a discrete valuation ring (or DVR) if there exists a discrete valuation v on its fraction field K = K(A) for which Ov = A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently any Noetherian regular local ring of dimension 1 with uniformizer t gives a valuation v defined by writing any nonzero element as u t^n and setting v(ut^n)=n. Exercises show converses: a DVR is a Noetherian regular local ring of dimension 1, and there is only one discrete valuation on a discrete valuation ring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeros and poles via valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the valuation of an element is n>0, the element has a zero of order n; if the valuation is -n<0, the element has a pole of order n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes precise the geometric notion of zeros/poles at regular codimension-1 points (where O_{X,p} is a DVR). The text warns this behaves less well at non-regular/non-codimension-1 points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: DVR ↔ Noetherian regular local ring of dimension 1 (and related equivalences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 12.5.6: An integral domain A is a Noetherian local ring of dimension 1 satisfying (a)–(d) if and only if (e) A is a discrete valuation ring. Theorem 12.5.8: for a Noetherian local ring of dimension 1, conditions (a)–(e) are equivalent to (f) A is a unique factorization domain and (g) A is integrally closed in its fraction field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches: express elements as u t^n to get valuation; converses use ideal structure and integrality arguments (reduce to A/(r) etc.). Exercises guide showing ideals are I_n = {r : v(r) ≥ n} and how uniqueness of factorization arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of zeros and poles on Noetherian schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 12.5.G: Suppose X is an integral Noetherian scheme and f ∈ K(X)^× is a nonzero element of its function field. Show that f has a finite number of zeros and poles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: reduce to X=Spec A and write f=f1/f2 with fi∈A and prove the result for the fi. This uses that valuations (DVRs) correspond to codimension-1 points in the Noetherian case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure theorem: finitely generated modules over a DVR
rubrics_metrics.description: Important remark 12.5.14: Any finitely generated module over a discrete valuation ring A with uniformizer t is a finite direct sum of terms A and A/(t^r) (for various r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the analogue of the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID, and is referenced for future consequences (see Proposition 13.7.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedekind domains and local DVR property
rubrics_metrics.description: A Dedekind domain is a Noetherian integral domain of dimension at most one that is normal (integrally closed). The localization of a Dedekind domain at any nonzero prime (a codimension-1 prime) is a discrete valuation ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rings of integers of number fields. One can prove unique factorization of ideals in a Dedekind domain: nonzero ideals factor uniquely into primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: smooth morphism (first definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 12.6.2: A morphism π : X → Y is smooth of relative dimension n if there exist open covers {Ui} of X and {Vi} of Y with π(Ui)⊂Vi, and for each i a commutative diagram identifying Ui∼→W (open in Spec B[x1,…,xn+r]/(f1,…,fr)) over Vi∼→Spec B, where the determinant of the Jacobian matrix (∂fj/∂xi)_{i,j≤r} is an invertible function on W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ´Etale means smooth of relative dimension 0. This definition is 'existence of local presentations with Jacobian determinant invertible' and is used to capture the local fibration intuition from differential geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences: basic properties of smooth morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: From the definition: smooth morphisms are locally of finite presentation (hence locally of finite type); the locus on X where π is smooth of relative dimension n is open; in particular the étale locus is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: open embeddings are étale; projection A^n_Y is smooth of relative dimension n. These quick observations inform how to check smoothness and behaviour under standard operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local and stability properties of smoothness
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness of relative dimension n is local on both source and target, preserved by base change, and composition adds relative dimensions: if π:X→Z is smooth of dim n and ρ:Y→Z is smooth of dim m then X×_Z Y → Z is smooth of dim m+n. In particular compositions and products of smooth (resp. étale) morphisms are smooth (resp. étale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 12.6.B–12.6.D and 12.6.C–D guide these verifications. There is an exercise showing local factorization of any smooth morphism into an étale map followed by projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence with smoothness over a field
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 12.6.4: For a k-scheme X, X is smooth of relative dimension n over Spec k (Definition 12.6.2) if and only if X has pure dimension n and is smooth over k in the earlier sense (Definition 12.2.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Jacobian corank, Zariski tangent space dimension bounds, and localization arguments. This shows the new definition specializes correctly to the field case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuative criterion for separatedness (DVR version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 12.7.1: Suppose π : X → Y is a morphism of finite type of locally Noetherian schemes. Then π is separated iff for any discrete valuation ring A and any diagram Spec K(A) → X over Y, there is at most one morphism Spec A → X making the diagram commute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: Spec A is a 'germ of a curve' and Spec K(A) the 'germ minus origin'; the criterion captures uniqueness of limits of one-parameter families. An easy direction (if π separated then criterion holds) is Exercise 12.7.A; the other direction is sketched via constructing DVRs from failure of separatedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: General valuative criterion for separatedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 12.7.4: Suppose π : X → Y is a quasi-separated morphism. Then π is separated iff for any valuation ring A with function field K and any diagram Spec K → X over Y, there is at most one morphism Spec A → X completing the diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the DVR version by allowing arbitrary valuation rings. References: Stacks project tags and EGA for full proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuative criterion for universal closedness and properness (DVR version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 12.7.6: Suppose π : X → Y is a morphism of finite type of locally Noetherian schemes. Then π is universally closed (resp. proper) iff for any DVR A and diagram Spec K(A) → X over Y there is at least one (resp. exactly one) morphism Spec A → X making the diagram commute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation when Y is a field: limits of one-parameter families in proper varieties always exist and are unique. Use together with the criterion for separatedness to characterize properness.

rubrics_metrics.name: General valuative criterion for universal closedness and properness
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 12.7.9: Suppose π : X → Y is quasi-separated, finite type (hence quasi-compact). Then π is universally closed (resp. proper) iff for any valuation ring A and diagram Spec K → X over Y, there is at least one (resp. exactly one) morphism Spec A → X completing the diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the valuation-ring generalization of the DVR criterion and references Stacks/EGA for proofs. The three valuative criteria (separatedness, universal closedness, properness) form a family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moduli interpretation of valuative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: If Y=Spec k and X is a fine moduli space of objects, separatedness means at most one way to extend a family over a punctured DVR, and properness means precisely one way (existence+uniqueness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a concrete moduli-theoretic meaning to the abstract valuative criteria; see Remarks 12.7.2 and 12.7.7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings: localization preserves regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact 12.8.2: If (A,m) is a regular local ring, then any localization of A at a prime is also a regular local ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This deep theorem (proved by Serre/Auslander-Buchsbaum using homological methods) implies for Noetherian schemes one can check regularity at closed points. The text will prove two important cases later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings are UFDs, integrally closed, and Cohen–Macaulay
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact (Auslander–Buchsbaum Theorem 12.8.5): Regular local rings are unique factorization domains. Consequences: regular local rings are integrally closed; they are Cohen–Macaulay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are nontrivial facts (some proofs deferred). The text gives examples showing factoriality is strictly weaker than regularity and discusses geometric consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of I‑filtrations and Rees algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: 12.9.1: For an ideal I in A, an I‑filtration of an A‑module M is a descending filtration M = M0 ⊃ M1 ⊃ M2 ⊃ … with I·Mn ⊂ Mn+1. The Rees algebra A•(I) = ⊕_{n≥0} I^n and the graded module M•=⊕_{n≥0} Mn turn filtrations into graded modules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An I‑filtration is I‑stable if IdMs = Ms+d for all d≥0 for some s. The Rees algebra/module viewpoint is used to prove Artin–Rees-type statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artin–Rees type proposition: finite generation ⇔ I‑stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 12.9.2: If A is Noetherian and M a finitely generated A‑module, then the graded module M• is a finitely generated A•(I)-module iff the filtration (M_n) is I‑stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: Noetherianness of A•(I) implies stabilization of certain chains; conversely I‑stability gives finite generation of the graded module. This sets up Artin–Rees Lemma used later.
